title: How do you safely evolve a contract used by many services — prefer additive changes with a compatibility window (new fields optional, deprecate-before-delete, provider contract tests), watch for semantic (not just structural) breaks, and treat a Kafka event as a durable integration contract (schema evolution + backward compatibility for replay) rather than publishing internal JPA entities/DTOs directly?
shortTitle: How do you safely evolve a contract used by many services

s1_definition.profdef: Safely evolving a shared contract means changing a schema that many independent services depend on without forcing them all to change at once. The safe pattern is additive change with a compatibility window: new fields are optional with defaults, you deprecate before you delete, and you verify compatibility with provider contract tests. You must watch for semantic breaks, where the structure is unchanged but the meaning of a value changes, which is more dangerous than a structural break because tests still pass. For asynchronous integration, a Kafka event is a durable contract that may be replayed long after it was written, so you use a schema registry with backward-compatible evolution and you never publish internal JPA entities or DTOs directly, publishing a stable, deliberately designed event schema instead.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India sends a standard "money transferred" notice that twenty different departments read. If you suddenly change what a field means, every department quietly misreads it and nobody gets an error, which is worse than an obvious breakage. So the bank only ever adds optional new lines, keeps the meaning of existing lines fixed, announces well in advance before removing anything, and keeps a copy of the exact notice format in a central rulebook so old archived notices can still be understood years later. The bank never just photocopies its private internal ledger page and mails it out, because then its internal mess becomes everyone's problem.
s1_definition.oneliner: Only add optional fields, never change the meaning of existing ones, deprecate before you delete, verify with contract tests, and treat a Kafka event as a stable published schema in a registry, never your internal entity.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Safely evolving a shared contract means changing a schema that many independent services depend on without forcing them all to change at once. The safe pattern is additive change with a compatibility window: new fields are optional with defaults, you deprecate before you delete, and you verify compatibility with provider contract tests. You must watch for semantic breaks, where the structure is unchanged but the meaning of a value changes, which is more dangerous than a structural break because tests still pass. For asynchronous integration, a Kafka event is a durable contract that may be replayed long after it was written, so you use a schema registry with backward-compatible evolution and you never publish internal JPA entities or DTOs directly, publishing a stable, deliberately designed event schema instead.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India sends a standard "money transferred" notice that twenty different departments read. If you suddenly change what a field means, every department quietly misreads it and nobody gets an error, which is worse than an obvious breakage. So the bank only ever adds optional new lines, keeps the meaning of existing lines fixed, announces well in advance before removing anything, and keeps a copy of the exact notice format in a central rulebook so old archived notices can still be understood years later. The bank never just photocopies its private internal ledger page and mails it out, because then its internal mess becomes everyone's problem.

**One line to remember:** Only add optional fields, never change the meaning of existing ones, deprecate before you delete, verify with contract tests, and treat a Kafka event as a stable published schema in a registry, never your internal entity.

sections.s2_technical:
The foundation is backward and forward compatibility. Backward compatible means a new producer's output can still be read by old consumers; forward compatible means an old producer's output can still be read by new consumers. Additive changes, like adding an optional field with a default, are the safest because they preserve both directions: old consumers ignore the new field, and new consumers see the default when the field is absent. Removing a field, renaming it, changing its type, or making an optional field required all break one direction or both, so they are breaking changes that need a managed migration, not a silent edit.

The compatibility window is how you avoid a flag-day where everyone must deploy together. You add the new field first and ship it. Consumers migrate to it on their own schedule. Only in a later release, after you have confirmed no one depends on the old field, do you remove it. This is the expand-and-contract pattern, also called parallel change: expand by adding the new, let consumers switch, then contract by removing the old. Deprecate-before-delete means you mark the old field as deprecated, document the replacement, and give a concrete sunset, so removal is never a surprise.

Provider contract tests are how you catch breakage at build time instead of in production. In a consumer-driven contract approach, each consumer publishes the shape it actually relies on, and the provider's build runs those contracts against its current output. If the provider removes a field a consumer needs, the provider's build fails before deployment. This turns "we think it is safe" into "the build proves it is safe for every known consumer".

Semantic breaks are the dangerous ones precisely because they are invisible to structural checks. If a field called `amount` used to be in rupees and you change it to paise, the JSON shape is identical, every schema check passes, every contract test that only checks structure passes, and yet every consumer is now wrong by a factor of a hundred. The same happens if you change an enum value's meaning, change a timestamp from local time to UTC, or change a status code to now be returned in a new situation. The defence is discipline: never repurpose an existing field, introduce a new field with the new meaning instead, and encode units and semantics explicitly, for example a money object carrying its currency and minor-unit scale rather than a bare number.

Kafka events deserve the strictest treatment because they are durable. A REST response is consumed immediately, but an event can sit in a topic or be replayed from the beginning weeks or months later, so a consumer may legitimately read an event produced by a much older schema. You put the schema in a schema registry, use a format like Avro, Protobuf, or JSON Schema, and configure a compatibility mode, typically backward or full, so the registry refuses to register a schema that would break existing consumers. You add fields with defaults, never remove required fields, and you version the event type when a truly breaking change is unavoidable. Critically, you never publish your internal JPA entity or internal DTO straight to Kafka, because that couples every consumer to your database layout and means an innocent refactor of your entity silently changes the public contract. Instead you define an explicit event class, map your internal model to it deliberately, and treat that event class as a carefully governed published API.

Senior nuances: keep events small and intention-revealing, often carrying identifiers plus the changed facts rather than entire object graphs; prefer immutable, append-only event design; document the contract and own it like code; and version the topic or event type only as a last resort because, like API versions, every live event version is ongoing cost.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India publishes an `AccountCreditedEvent` to Kafka that many services consume, including statements, notifications, and analytics. The team needed to add the crediting channel, such as UPI or NEFT. This is exactly the additive case: a new optional field with a default keeps every existing consumer working.

Problem 2 — Someone proposed reusing the existing `amount` field, which was in rupees, to carry paise instead, to avoid decimals. This is exactly a semantic break: the structure is identical so every test passes, but every consumer would be wrong by a hundredfold. The safe path is a new explicitly-scaled money field, never repurposing the old one.

Problem 3 — The original code published the internal JPA `AccountEntity` straight to Kafka, so a later refactor that renamed a database column silently broke downstream consumers. This is exactly why you publish a deliberate event class mapped from the entity, not the entity itself.

Our mini-project demonstrates safe evolution. The code defines an internal `AccountEntity`, a published `AccountCreditedEvent` with a schema version and an added optional channel field, an `EventPublisher` that maps the entity to the event deliberately, a `ConsumerV1` written against the old schema, and a demo that publishes a v2 event and shows the old consumer still reads it correctly because the change was additive, while also showing why a semantic change would silently corrupt it.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's internal account entity SAV2001 and a credit of 50,000 rupees via UPI.

Step 1: The publisher receives the internal `AccountEntity`. It does not send that entity to Kafka. Instead it deliberately maps only the fields that belong in the public contract into a fresh `AccountCreditedEvent`, so a later refactor of the entity cannot silently change the public contract.

Step 2: During mapping the publisher sets the amount as an explicit money object carrying both the value and the currency, so there is no ambiguity about units. This is the guard against semantic breaks, because a consumer can never misinterpret rupees as paise when the currency and scale are explicit.

Step 3: The publisher also fills the new `channel` field, which was added in schema version 2. Because this field is optional with a safe default of absent, it is a backward-compatible additive change.

Step 4: The event is published. In production the schema registry, configured in backward-compatible mode, would have accepted this schema because the only change was an added optional field, and would have rejected it had someone tried to remove or retype a field.

Step 5: The old v1 consumer, which was written before `channel` existed, reads the event. It reads only the fields it knows, posts the statement line correctly, and simply ignores `channel`. It never crashes and never misreads anything, which proves the evolution was safe.

```
2026-10-24 14:42:11 INFO    PUBLISHED v2: AccountCreditedEvent{acc=SAV2001, amount=50000.00 INR, channel=UPI, at=1792...}
2026-10-24 14:42:11 INFO    V1 consumer posted statement line: credited 50000.00 INR to SAV2001 (channel ignored by v1)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Safely evolving a contract that many services depend on is about changing a shared schema without forcing everyone to deploy on the same day. The foundation is compatibility in both directions: backward compatible means a new producer's output is still readable by old consumers, and forward compatible means an old producer's output is still readable by new consumers. Additive changes, like adding an optional field with a default, preserve both directions because old consumers ignore what they do not know and new consumers fall back to the default, so I make those freely. Removing, renaming, retyping, or making an optional field required all break compatibility, so they need a managed migration, never a silent edit.

I run changes through a compatibility window using expand-and-contract. I add the new field first and ship it, let consumers migrate on their own schedule, and only remove the old field in a later release once I have confirmed no one depends on it. Deprecate-before-delete means I mark the old field deprecated, document its replacement, and give a concrete sunset so removal is never a surprise. I back all of this with provider contract tests, where each consumer publishes the shape it actually relies on and my build runs those contracts against my current output, so my build fails before deployment if I break a known consumer. That turns "we think it is safe" into "the build proves it is safe".

The subtle danger I always call out is the semantic break, where the structure is unchanged but the meaning changes, because then every schema check and structural contract test still passes while every consumer is silently wrong. The classic example is changing a field from rupees to paise, where the JSON looks identical but every amount is now off by a hundredfold. My defence is to never repurpose an existing field; I add a new field with the new meaning, and I encode units and semantics explicitly, for example a money object that carries its currency and scale instead of a bare number.

For asynchronous integration I treat a Kafka event as the strictest kind of contract, because it is durable and can be replayed months later, so a consumer may legitimately read an event written by a much older schema. I keep the schema in a schema registry with a backward or full compatibility mode so the registry itself refuses a breaking schema, I add fields with defaults and never remove required ones, and I version the event type only as a last resort. The mistake I have personally seen cause an outage is publishing an internal JPA entity straight to Kafka, because then an innocent column rename silently changed the public contract, so at National Bank of India we switched to mapping the entity into an explicit, deliberately governed event class.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I only add optional fields, never change the meaning of existing ones, deprecate before I delete, prove safety with provider contract tests, and treat every Kafka event as a stable published schema in a registry rather than my internal entity on the wire.
